To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
we have observed the pulsar J0437− 4715 at 192 MHz using the Murchison wide-field Array and have measured its low-frequency characteristics.
we have observed a millisecond pulsar at a low radio frequency (192 MHz), and we have detected the rapid intensity variations that arise from difractive scintillation in the interstellar plasma.

1) we observed PSR J04375–4715 with the 64-tile Murchison Wide-Field Array (MWA), 2) our observations show rapid modulatons of pulse intensity in both time and frequency, 3) the scattering screen is at ∼80-120 pc from the sun, and 4) the pulse profile evolves dramatically with frequency.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the interstellar medium, and its effect on the radio waves emitted by pulsars.
understanding the low-frequency behaviour of the millisecond radio pulsar PSR B1937+21.
the low-frequency characteristics of the millisecond radio pulsar PSR J0437−471 5, which is located in the direction of the Galactic anticenter and has a spin period of 5.76 ms.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
PSR J0435–6845 is not the best millisecond pulsar for the detection of gravitational waves.
the MWA has detected the pulsar and has observed its scintillations.
PSR J04375-4715 is the best known millisecond pulsar in the southern hemisphere.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the MWA has detected the millisecond pulsars PSR J0435-4720 and PSR J0436-4720 at 192 MHz and has detected the milli-second pulsar PSRJ0437-4715 at 192 MHz.
the MWA can detect millisecond pulsars with a signal-to-noise ratio of 10 within 1 hr of observation.

we have demonstrated that the low-frequency radio sky, which is dominated by the diffuse Galactic synchrotron emission, can be used for high precision astrophysical studies, such as the characterization of pulsar dispersion and scattering, and the study of pulsar magnetospheric emission.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, in order to accurately interpret the low-frequency observations, a detailed model of the ISM is required, which is beyond the scope of the current paper.

the MWA is capable of detecting millisecond pulsar signals with signal-to-noise ratios as low as ∼10, and that the MWA will be able to detect the majority of the known millisecond pulsars in the southern sky with similar sensitivity.

the MWA has already demonstrated the capability of making important contributions to the field of millisecond pulsar timing, and that the next generation of low-frequency radio telescopes, like the Low-Frequency Array (LOFAR) and the Square Kilometer Array (SKA) low-frequency component, will be able to probe the ISM in unprecedented detail.
